explainers.title: Welcome back to Global Perspectives
explainers.body:
Hello, and welcome to Unit 3 of Global Perspectives at Ehel Academy. By now you know that this subject is not about memorising facts for a test. It grows a set of thinking skills you can carry into any subject, any job, and any decision you will ever make. This unit trains one of the sharpest of them all: Evaluation.

There are six skills in Global Perspectives, and you keep growing all of them, year after year:

In Unit 1 you learned to research a topic, and in Unit 2 you learned to analyse it. Now comes the skill that keeps you from being fooled. Every day you meet claims that sound true: an advert, a video, a headline, a friend repeating something they read online. Evaluation is how you decide which of them to believe. In Stage 8 you go further than before. You will judge sources not only for whether they can be trusted, but for whether their evidence really proves the point. You will spot bias and hidden interests, weigh two opposing arguments against each other, and reach a balanced judgement that you can justify with reasons.

Why does this matter beyond school? Think of the choices adults weigh every week. A voter decides which promise to believe. A parent reads two very different articles about a new medicine. A shopkeeper is told a product will 'sell itself'. Each of them is really evaluating: asking who is speaking, why, and whether the evidence holds up. The learner who practises this now will be much harder to mislead for the rest of their life. That is the power of this unit.
bullets: Research — finding things out about the world in a careful, organised way.
Analysis — taking a topic apart to see its causes, effects and connections.
Evaluation — judging how strong a source, an argument or a piece of evidence really is.
Reflection — thinking honestly about how you learn and how your views change.
Collaboration — working well with other people towards a shared goal.
Communication — sharing your ideas so clearly that others truly understand.

explainers.title: How you will learn this unit
explainers.body:
You are learning the Ehel Academy way, which is self-paced. Three kinds of support work together, and in Stage 8 you take a little more of the lead yourself:

Older versions of this subject told learners to 'talk to a partner' or 'discuss with the class'. In our model, your AI tutor is your partner and your class. So every 'Ask Your AI Tutor' box is a real conversation. Evaluation grows fastest when someone pushes back on your thinking, so ask the tutor to disagree with you on purpose and see whether your judgement still holds.
bullets: You, learning at your own pace. You read, think and complete each activity in your own time. Slow down where an idea is hard; move quickly where it is easy. You decide the order and the speed.

Your AI tutor, available every hour of the day. Wherever this book says 'Ask Your AI Tutor', you talk to your tutor as if it were a thoughtful study partner and a whole class rolled into one. It discusses your ideas, questions your thinking, plays devil's advocate, and gives feedback whenever you are ready, day or night.
Your teacher, about twice a week. In live sessions you bring your best judgements and your sharpest questions, hear how other learners weighed the same evidence, and get guidance on where to go next.

explainers.title: Meet Maya, our evaluator for this unit
explainers.body:
To make every skill concrete, we will follow one Year 8 learner through the whole unit. Her name is Maya, and she studies at Ehel Academy in Hargeisa.

A new shop has opened near Maya's school gate, and it sells brightly coloured energy drinks. The posters promise the drinks will 'sharpen your mind for exams'. Her friends share a video of a famous footballer who supposedly 'drinks six a day', and several classmates now buy one before every study session. But the school nurse warns that the drinks ruin sleep and give students a crash an hour later. Maya notices something interesting: the very same claim, that energy drinks help students study, is told in completely different ways depending on who is speaking, and who stands to make money.

That puzzle becomes Maya's Challenge for this unit: should students at Ehel Academy believe that energy drinks help them study? To answer it honestly she cannot just pick the side she likes. She has to evaluate: judge each source, test each fact, spot who is biased, weigh the arguments on both sides, and reach a judgement she can defend. You will watch her do exactly that, skill by skill, and you will do the same with a Challenge of your own.

explainers.title: Your Challenge: the project that runs through the unit
explainers.body:
This unit builds towards one ongoing project we call your Challenge. For an Evaluation unit, the best Challenge is a question where thoughtful people genuinely disagree and where different sources tell you different things. That gives you real evidence to weigh and a real judgement to reach.

Here are some issues where the sources disagree and where you will have to decide who to believe. Any of these could become your Challenge:

You do not have to choose yet. As you work through the skills, keep a note of any claim that made you think 'is that really true?' A claim you are unsure about is the perfect Challenge, because evaluation is exactly the skill for deciding.
bullets: Do energy drinks or sugary drinks really help, or harm, students?
Is a viral health or safety story spreading online true, or is it fake news?
Should a green space in town be built on, or protected?
Do mobile phones help or harm learning in school?
Is a heavily advertised product as good as its advert claims?
Should plastic bags be banned, and what do the different sides really argue?
Is a particular news source reliable, or does it lean to one side?
Does a popular online influencer give trustworthy advice?

explainers.title: What is evaluation, really?
explainers.body:
Many people think 'evaluation' just means saying whether you liked something. Real evaluation is far more careful. Evaluation is weighing the strengths and weaknesses of a source, an argument or a piece of evidence, so that you can judge how far it can be trusted, and then reaching a fair overall judgement. It always ends in a decision, and that decision is always backed by reasons.

Good evaluation moves through a cycle. At Stage 8 the cycle is more demanding than simply asking 'do I believe this?':

You will learn every step in this unit. Notice that 'do I agree?' is not on the list. A good evaluator can judge a source strong even when it argues against them, and weak even when it argues for their side. Fairness comes first; the verdict comes last.
bullets: Read or watch the source closely, and find exactly what it is claiming.
Ask who made it and why: its author and its purpose.
Check its reliability: can it be trusted, and do other good sources agree?
Check its validity: does its evidence actually prove the claim it is making?
Look for bias and vested interest that might tilt it to one side.
Test the argument: are the reasons and evidence strong, and do they make sense?
Weigh it against the other side and any competing arguments.
Reach a balanced judgement, and justify it with your strongest reasons.

explainers.title: Evaluation is not the same as analysis
explainers.body:
People often mix up analysis and evaluation, so it is worth being clear. Analysis breaks a thing into its parts to understand it. Evaluation then judges how good those parts are. Analysis asks 'what is this made of, and how does it work?' Evaluation asks 'how strong is it, and can I trust it?'

For example, if you analyse an advert you might say: it makes one claim, gives one reason, and shows a photo of a smiling student. If you then evaluate it you might say: the claim is not backed by real evidence, the photo proves nothing, and the company has a reason to exaggerate, so the advert is weak. Analysis describes; evaluation judges. You need both, and evaluation almost always comes after analysis.

explainers.title: Keep an evaluation journal
explainers.body:
Before you meet the first skill, start a habit that careful thinkers use: keep an evaluation journal. This is a notebook or document where, for each source you meet in your Challenge, you record who made it, what it claims, and how much you trust it and why. Write the date each time, and note how your judgement changes as you find more evidence.

A journal matters for three reasons. It keeps your judgements and reasons in one place, so you never have to rely on memory. It shows how your thinking changed, which you will need later for Reflection. And it makes your final judgement far easier to justify, because your evidence is already gathered. Keep your journal beside you as you read the rest of this file.

explainers.title: Skill 1 (3.1): Judging a source by its author and purpose
explainers.body:
The first move in evaluating any source is to ask two questions before you even judge the content: who made this, and why? These are the source's author and its purpose. A source is not automatically wrong because it wants something, but you should always know what it wants.

Once you know the author and purpose, you read the source differently. A page written by a health organisation to inform families is read as trustworthy but still checkable. An advert written by a company to sell a drink is read with your guard up, because its purpose is to persuade, not to balance.
bullets: Author — who wrote or made it? Are they named? Do they really know the topic? Are they a real person or organisation you have heard of?
Purpose — why was it made? To inform you fairly, to persuade you, to sell you something, to entertain, or to push one point of view?

explainers.title: Skill 2 (3.1): Reliability and validity are two different questions
explainers.body:
At Stage 8 you learn to ask two separate questions about a source, not one. A reliable source can be trusted to be true and accurate. A valid piece of evidence actually proves the particular claim it is being used for. A source can be reliable but used invalidly, so you must check both.

This difference is powerful. Suppose an advert says: 'Our drink contains vitamins, so it helps you study.' The fact that the drink contains vitamins might be perfectly reliable, yet it is not valid evidence for studying better, because containing a vitamin does not mean it improves concentration. Spotting that gap is exactly the sharper thinking Stage 8 asks of you.
bullets: Reliability asks: Is this true and trustworthy? Who made it, are they expert, is it evidence-based, do other good sources agree, is it up to date?
Validity asks: Even if this fact is true, does it really support the claim? A true fact can be dragged in to 'prove' something it does not prove.

explainers.title: Skill 3 (3.1): Spotting fake news and checking whether a fact is real
explainers.body:
Fake news is false information that is deliberately created to trick people into believing it is true, often for political or business reasons. It is not the same as an honest mistake; it is made to deceive. Because fake stories are designed to look real, you cannot judge them by how convincing they feel. You have to check.

A piece of information that looks like a fact may be real or made up. The most powerful test is simple: try to find the same fact in more than one trusted source. If a striking 'fact' appears on only one unknown website and nowhere else, be very careful. Here are the questions careful checkers ask:
bullets: Has this fact been reported anywhere else, especially by well-known sources?
Have I actually heard of the author or organisation reporting it?
Does the website look real, and is there a named, real author?
Does the fact serve someone's purpose, such as selling a product or scoring a point?
Is there anything odd about the source, the spelling, or the date?

explainers.title: Skill 4 (3.1): Fact, opinion, and how strong each is as evidence
explainers.body:
To judge evidence well, you must tell a fact from an opinion. A fact is something that can be checked and proven to be true. An opinion is what someone thinks or believes, which others could reasonably disagree with. Both can be used as evidence, but they are not equally strong.

Opinions are not worthless. The opinion of an expert, backed by facts, can be valuable. But an opinion with no facts behind it, however strongly it is stated, proves very little. When you evaluate a source, sort its sentences: which are facts you could check, and which are opinions dressed up to sound like facts?
bullets: Fact — can be proven true, so it is stronger evidence. Example: a study measured that this drink contains a large amount of sugar.
Opinion — cannot be proven, so it is weaker evidence on its own. Example: this drink tastes amazing and everyone should try it.

explainers.title: Skill 5 (3.1): Detecting bias and vested interest
explainers.body:
Bias is when a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced. A biased source often gives only the points that suit its view and hides the rest. Closely linked is vested interest: when the person or group behind a source stands to gain, usually money, power or reputation, from you believing them. Vested interest is one of the biggest causes of bias.

A source is not automatically wrong because it is biased or has an interest, but you must notice it and balance it. A one-sided argument, for example, gives only the advantages of something and never the disadvantages. When you see only good points and no drawbacks, ask what is being left out, and who benefits.
bullets: Signs of bias — only one side is shown, strong emotional words, drawbacks ignored, opponents mocked rather than answered.
Signs of vested interest — the source sells the very thing it praises, or gains status or money if you agree.

explainers.title: Skill 6 (3.1): How purpose and audience shape a text
explainers.body:
Every text is made for a purpose and aimed at an audience, and both change what it says and what it leaves out. Texts can inform, persuade, advise, argue, describe, entertain or instruct. The same topic will be written very differently depending on why it was made and who it is for. A good evaluator reads the purpose and audience before trusting the content.

Knowing this protects you from a common mistake: thinking that any text with a purpose must be lying. That is not true. A text can have a purpose and still be honest. The skill is to match your trust to the purpose, and to notice when a persuading text quietly drops the facts that do not help it.

explainers.title: Skill 7 (3.2): What an argument is - claim, reason and evidence
explainers.body:
To evaluate an argument, you first have to see its parts. In Global Perspectives, an argument is a reason or set of reasons put forward to justify a claim, a perspective or an action, usually supported by evidence. It is built from three pieces:

A claim on its own is just an assertion. It becomes an argument only when reasons and evidence are added. When you evaluate, you separate the three parts, then ask of each: is the claim clear, does the reason actually justify the claim, and is the evidence real and relevant? A claim is often used as a headline, so learn to look underneath it for the reasons and evidence, or their absence.
bullets: Claim — a statement that something is true. It answers the question: What do I think?
Reason — why the claim should be believed. It answers the question: Why do I think this?
Evidence — facts, studies, examples or quotations that back up the reason. It answers: How do I know this?

explainers.title: Skill 8 (3.2): How effective is the argument? Testing the reasoning
explainers.body:
Once you can see an argument's parts, you can judge its effectiveness: how well it actually holds together. A source's argument should make sense if it is to be trusted. At Stage 8 you learn to name the common ways reasoning goes wrong, so you can point to the exact weakness instead of just feeling unsure.

An effective argument, by contrast, states a clear claim, gives reasons that truly justify it, backs them with reliable and relevant evidence, and is honest about the other side. When you evaluate, judge the structure and the evidence together: a well-organised argument built on weak evidence is still a weak argument.
bullets: One-sided — it gives only the advantages and never the disadvantages, so it is not the full picture.
Unsupported — it makes a big claim but offers no real evidence, only strong words.
The reason does not fit — the reason given does not actually justify the claim being made.
The evidence does not prove it — the evidence is real but does not support this particular claim (a validity problem).

explainers.title: Skill 9 (3.2): Weighing two competing arguments against each other
explainers.body:
Most real issues have strong arguments on more than one side. The Stage 8 skill is not to pick your favourite, but to place the two arguments side by side and weigh them: which has the clearer claim, the better reasons, the more reliable and valid evidence, and the fewer hidden interests? You compare like a pair of scales, point against point.

To weigh fairly, judge both sides by the same tests. It helps to build a simple grid: for each argument, note the main claim, the strongest reason, the quality of the evidence, the reliability of the source, and any bias or vested interest. Only when both columns are filled in can you honestly say which side is stronger, and by how much.

explainers.title: Skill 10 (3.1 and 3.2): Reaching and justifying a balanced judgement
explainers.body:
Evaluation is not finished until you reach a judgement and justify it. A judgement is your overall decision: which source or argument is stronger, and what you now believe. Justifying means giving the reasons for that decision, drawn from all the evaluating you have done. A balanced judgement is honest about the other side; it does not pretend the losing argument had nothing in it.

A strong justified judgement usually does four things: it states the decision clearly, it names the strongest evidence behind it, it acknowledges the best point from the other side, and it explains why your side still wins overall. This is what turns evaluation from an opinion into a defendable conclusion.

explainers.title: How evaluation feeds the other five skills
explainers.body:
Evaluation is placed in the middle of the six skills for a reason: it sharpens all the others. Once you can judge how strong a source or argument is, everything else improves.

So the effort you put into evaluation now is never wasted. It is the skill that keeps all the others honest.
bullets: Research gets better, because you gather only sources you have judged trustworthy.
Analysis gets deeper, because you can tell a strong cause-and-effect claim from a weak one.
Reflection grows every time you notice a judgement you got wrong and why.
Collaboration works better when everyone can weigh evidence fairly instead of just arguing.
Communication becomes powerful, because a judgement you can justify is far more convincing than an opinion you cannot.

explainers.title: Putting it all together: the evaluation cycle
explainers.body: You have now met every evaluation skill in this unit. Here is how they fit into one cycle you can use on any source or argument:
bullets: Find the claim: what is this source really saying?
Ask who made it and why, its author and purpose.
Check reliability: can it be trusted, and do others agree?
Check validity: does the evidence actually prove the claim?
Spot bias and vested interest, and sort fact from opinion.
Test the argument: are the reasons and evidence strong, and do they make sense?
Weigh it against the other side.
Reach a balanced judgement, and justify it with your best reasons.

explainers.title: What comes next
explainers.body: The next unit is Reflection. Once you can evaluate sources and arguments, reflection teaches you to turn that judging eye on your own thinking: to notice how your views changed, where you were fooled, and how you learn best. Strong evaluation now makes honest reflection much easier later. Well done for building the skill that keeps you from being misled.

bigIdeas.title: One big idea to hold on to
lines: In Global Perspectives, the topic is the vehicle and the skill is the destination.
We will travel through real issues such as health claims, adverts, news stories and online videos.
But the aim is not to become an expert on energy drinks or fake news. The aim is to become a person who can judge almost any claim, fairly and well.

bigIdeas.title: A quick test: is this analysis or evaluation?
lines: Analysis: The article gives three reasons and quotes one scientist.
Evaluation: The article is weak because two of its reasons have no evidence.
If the sentence describes the parts, it is analysis. If it judges how good they are, it is evaluation.
A useful sign of evaluation is a judging word: strong, weak, reliable, biased, convincing, one-sided.

bigIdeas.title: The two-question habit
lines: Question one, reliability: Can I trust that this is true?
Question two, validity: Even if it is true, does it prove the point being made?
Weak thinkers ask only the first. Strong Stage 8 evaluators always ask both.

bigIdeas.title: Trusted sources you have probably heard of
lines: Well-known news agencies, such as the BBC and Al Jazeera.
Established newspapers with named journalists and editors.
Global organisations such as the United Nations and the World Health Organization.
If a big claim appears nowhere in sources like these, treat it as unproven until it does.

bigIdeas.title: Same purpose, different audiences, still fair
lines: A poster for an Eid market and a poster for a Christmas market both have the same purpose: to attract shoppers.
Each is aimed at a different audience, but neither is dishonest simply for promoting its own event.
Having a purpose is normal. Bias only appears when a text hides the truth or is unfair to the other side.
Evaluate the honesty of a text, not just the fact that it wants something.

bigIdeas.title: A frame for a justified judgement
lines: State it: Having weighed both sides, I judge that ...
Support it: My strongest reason is ..., backed by ...
Be fair: I accept that the other side is right that ...
Decide: However, on balance the stronger case is ..., because ...

bigIdeas.title: Signs of a more reliable source
lines: It is a well-known news agency, newspaper or global organisation.
It has a named, real author or a clear organisation behind it.
It gives evidence, and other trusted sources agree with it.
It is up to date, and it is honest about the other side of the issue.

bigIdeas.title: Your Challenge runs through everything
lines: Pick one question where thoughtful people disagree and different sources tell you different things. This is your Challenge.
You will build on it in every activity, so choose something you genuinely want to get to the bottom of.
By the end you will have a balanced, justified judgement you can share with your teacher.

bigIdeas.title: Clues that a fact might be fake
lines: It appears on only one unknown website and nowhere trusted.
There is no named, real author, and the page is full of adverts.
It serves an obvious purpose, such as selling a product.
It sounds too dramatic, and no major news source mentions it.

bigIdeas.title: What makes a judgement balanced
lines: It states a clear decision, not a vague 'both sides are fine'.
It rests on the strongest evidence, not on the side you liked first.
It names at least one fair point from the other side.
It explains why your side still wins overall.

models.title: Evaluation happens in everyday life too
lines: Imagine two shopkeepers both tell you their phone chargers are 'the best in the market'.
You do not just believe the friendlier one. You evaluate.
You ask who is speaking and why: both want a sale, so both have an interest.
You test the evidence: one shows a warranty card and lets you try it; the other only repeats the word best.
You reach a judgement: the charger with real evidence is the safer buy. That is evaluation, and you already do it.

So evaluation is not a strange school-only activity. It is the everyday skill of not being fooled, done on purpose and with more care. In this unit you will simply learn to do it deliberately, with the same steps a journalist or a scientist would use.

models.title: Maya's example: two sources, two purposes
lines: Source one: a poster from the drinks shop. Author: the company that sells the drink. Purpose: to sell more drinks.
Source two: a page from a national health service. Author: named doctors. Purpose: to inform families about health.
Same topic, but Maya reads them very differently. The shop poster has every reason to hide the downsides; the health page has no drink to sell.
Maya does not throw the poster away, but she notes its purpose in her journal and looks much harder for evidence before she trusts it.

models.title: Karim's example: true but not valid
lines: Karim finds a claim: This energy drink is the number one seller in the country, so it must be good for students.
He checks reliability: the sales figure may well be true and come from a real report.
He checks validity: does being the best seller prove it is good for studying? No. Popular is not the same as healthy or helpful.
So Karim keeps the fact but rejects the argument. The evidence is reliable but invalid for this claim.

models.title: Maya's example: checking the footballer claim
lines: The viral claim: a famous footballer drinks six energy drinks a day and says they made him a star.
Maya searches for it in trusted sources: no major sports site or news agency reports it at all.
The only page carrying it is an unknown site with no author, covered in adverts for the same drink.
The claim serves an obvious purpose: selling drinks. Maya judges it very likely fake and keeps it out of her evidence.

models.title: Leila's example: sorting fact from opinion
lines: Leila reads: This is the healthiest drink on the shelf, and it contains 40 grams of sugar per can.
Fact, checkable: it contains 40 grams of sugar per can.
Opinion, not proven: it is the healthiest drink on the shelf.
Leila notices the opinion is doing the persuading, while the one real fact actually points the other way.

models.title: Maya's example: following the interest
lines: Maya lists who is behind each source on energy drinks.
The shop poster and the influencer video are paid by, or sell, the drink. They have a clear vested interest in the good news.
The school nurse and the health service gain nothing whether Maya buys the drink or not.
Maya does not dismiss the sellers automatically, but she trusts the sources with no vested interest to give her the fuller, fairer picture.

models.title: Omar's example: reading purpose and audience
lines: Omar compares two texts about a new road in Mogadishu. One is a council leaflet for residents; one is a builder's brochure for investors.
The leaflet's purpose is to inform residents and calm worries. The brochure's purpose is to persuade investors to fund it.
Knowing this, Omar expects the brochure to stress profit and hide problems, and reads it with extra care.
He does not reject either, but he checks the brochure's claims against a source with no money at stake.

models.title: Nadia's example: breaking an argument into parts
lines: Nadia reads: Students should drink this before exams (claim), because it keeps them awake to revise (reason), and a survey found 8 in 10 users felt more alert (evidence).
She checks each part. The claim is clear. The reason does connect to the claim.
But the evidence is weak: felt more alert is an opinion from users of the product, not a proper study of exam results.
So Nadia can name exactly where the argument is strong and where it is thin.

models.title: Rami's example: naming the flaw
lines: Rami reads: Everyone at my school drinks it, so it must be good for studying.
He tests the reasoning. The claim is that it is good for studying. The reason is that everyone drinks it.
But popularity does not justify the claim: lots of people can share a habit that does not help them.
Rami names the flaw precisely: the reason does not fit the claim. That is far stronger than saying I just do not buy it.

models.title: Maya's example: weighing both sides
lines: Argument A, from the shop and an influencer: the drinks help students study, because they keep you awake; evidence is user reviews.
Argument B, from the school nurse and a health service: the drinks harm study, because they wreck sleep and cause a crash; evidence is medical research.
Maya weighs them: both claims are clear, but B's evidence is more reliable and valid, and A's sources have a vested interest.
The scales tip towards B, though Maya notes A has a small fair point: a tired student may feel a short boost.

models.title: Maya's example: her justified judgement
lines: Having weighed both sides, Maya judges that energy drinks do not truly help students study.
Her strongest reason: the health sources, which have no vested interest, show the drinks harm sleep and focus, and their evidence is medical research, not adverts.
She is fair to the other side: a very tired student may feel a short-lived boost.
But on balance the harm outweighs it, so her judgement stands, and she can defend every part of it.

models.title: Maya's whole journey, from puzzle to judgement
lines: Skills 1 and 6: She read the author, purpose and audience of every source, from shop poster to health page.
Skills 2 and 4: She separated reliability from validity, and fact from opinion.
Skill 3: She checked the viral footballer 'fact' and found it was very likely fake.
Skill 5: She followed the vested interests and saw who gained from the good news.
Skills 7 and 8: She broke each argument into claim, reason and evidence, and named the flaws.
Skills 9 and 10: She weighed both sides and reached a balanced, justified judgement she can defend.

By following this cycle, Maya turned a confusing pile of claims into a clear, fair judgement backed by reasons. In the Activities file you will run the same cycle on your own Challenge, one step at a time, with your AI tutor beside you the whole way.

models.title: A model: Maya rates one source
lines: Source: the shop poster, made by the drinks company, purpose to sell drinks.
Reliability: low, because it is unsigned, gives no real evidence, and no trusted source backs it.
Validity: low, because containing vitamins does not prove better exam results.
Maya writes both reasons in her journal, so her final judgement will be easy to defend.

models.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Claim: Students should not drink energy drinks before exams.
Reason: because they disturb sleep, which harms memory.
Evidence: a health study measured worse sleep after drinking them.
Judgement: the reason fits the claim and the evidence is reliable, so this part of the argument is strong.

models.title: A model: reading a finished grid
lines: Argument A, from the sellers: clear claim, reason keeps you awake, evidence only user reviews, source has a vested interest.
Argument B, from a health service: clear claim, reason harms sleep, evidence medical research, source has nothing to sell.
Judged by the same tests, Argument B is stronger overall.
The fair point kept from A: a very tired student may feel a short boost before the crash.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Say hello to your AI tutor and tell it: I am starting Unit 3 of Stage 8 Global Perspectives, and the skill is Evaluation.
Ask it: What is the difference between analysing a source and evaluating it?
Then tell the tutor about one time you believed something online that turned out to be untrue, and ask what warning signs you might have missed.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor, in your own words, what you now think evaluation means.
Ask it: Is my definition missing anything important?
Then ask the tutor to give you one everyday example where evaluating a claim carefully would save someone from being tricked.

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe one source from your Challenge to your AI tutor: who made it, and why you think they made it.
Ask the tutor whether the purpose is mainly to inform, to persuade, or to sell.
Then ask: How should knowing the purpose change how carefully I check this source?

tutorPrompts.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Give your AI tutor one fact from a source in your Challenge, and the claim it is used to support.

toolkit.title: The evaluation cycle at a glance
toolkit.intro: Whatever the source, good evaluation follows the same eight steps. Come back to this list whenever you feel unsure about what to believe.
items: Claim: find what the source is really saying.
Author and purpose: ask who made it and why.
Reliability: can it be trusted, and do other good sources agree?
Validity: does the evidence actually prove the claim?
Bias: look for one-sidedness, vested interest, and fact dressed up as opinion.
Argument: test whether the reasons and evidence are strong and make sense.
Weigh: compare it against the other side.
Judge: reach a balanced judgement, and justify it with reasons.

toolkit.title: The Evaluation skill, in plain words
toolkit.intro:
Evaluation is weighing the strengths and weaknesses of a source, an argument or a piece of evidence, so that you can judge how far it can be trusted, and then reaching a fair overall judgement that you can justify. It is not just saying whether you liked something, and it is not the same as analysis, which only describes the parts.

Two habits sit at the heart of it. First, always ask who is speaking and why before you trust what they say. Second, always judge the evidence, not the side you prefer, and be ready to give your reasons. If you remember nothing else, remember those two habits.

toolkit.title: Cambridge Stage 8 Evaluation objectives
toolkit.intro: Global Perspectives sets out exactly what strong evaluation looks like at this stage. Here are the official Evaluation objectives, restated simply. Your teacher may refer to these codes.

rows: Evaluate sources, considering the author and purpose, recognising that some sources may be biased.
Judge how much to trust a source by asking who made it and why, and spotting bias and vested interest.
Discuss the effectiveness of a source, making explicit reference to its development of an argument.
Judge how good a source's argument is: find its claim, reasons and evidence, and say how well they hold together.

toolkit.title: Template: Reliability and validity checklist
toolkit.intro: Ask these questions about every source. The first group checks whether it is true; the second checks whether it proves its point.

rows: Who made it, and are they a named expert?
Do other trusted sources agree with it?
Is it up to date, with no odd errors or dates?
Does it give real evidence, not just strong words?
Even if the facts are true, do they prove this claim?
Is the evidence relevant to the exact point being made?

toolkit.title: Template: Bias and vested-interest spotting
toolkit.intro: Use this to decide whether a source is leaning to one side, and who gains if you agree.

rows: Does it show only one side of the issue?
Does it ignore obvious drawbacks or opposite points?
Does it use strong, emotional words to persuade?
Does the source sell, or gain from, what it praises?
Who benefits if I believe this source?
Where could I find a fair source from the other side?

toolkit.title: Template: Argument-weighing grid
toolkit.intro: Copy this grid whenever you must weigh two opposing arguments. Judge both by the same tests, then compare the columns.

rows: Main claim
Strongest reason
Quality of evidence
Reliability of source
Any bias or vested interest
Overall strength

toolkit.title: Template: The judgement-justification frame
toolkit.intro: When you have weighed the evidence, use this four-part frame to write a balanced judgement you can defend.
items: State it: Having weighed both sides, I judge that ...
Support it: My strongest reason is ..., backed by the evidence that ...
Be fair: I accept that the other side is right that ...
Decide: However, on balance the stronger case is ..., because ...

toolkit.title: Fact and opinion
toolkit.intro: A fact is usually stronger evidence than an opinion. An expert opinion backed by facts can still be useful, but an opinion with no facts behind it proves very little, however strongly it is stated. When you read a source, try underlining the facts you could check in one colour and the opinions in another; it quickly shows you how much real evidence the source is actually built on.

rows: Fact
Something that can be checked and proven to be true.
This can contains 40 grams of sugar.
Opinion
What someone thinks or believes, which others could dispute.
This is the best drink for students.

toolkit.title: The three parts of an argument
toolkit.intro: A claim on its own is only an assertion. It becomes an argument when a reason and evidence are added. When you evaluate, check that the reason truly justifies the claim, and that the evidence is real and relevant. A common trick is to state a claim loudly and hope you will not notice that the reason and evidence are missing, so always look underneath the claim for the two parts that should support it.

rows: Claim
A statement that something is true.
What do I think?
Reason
Why the claim should be believed.
Why do I think this?
Evidence
Facts, studies, examples or quotations that back the reason.
How do I know this?

toolkit.title: Reliable and unreliable sources
toolkit.intro: A reliable source can be trusted to be true; an unreliable source cannot. You are more likely to have heard of reliable sources, and you can usually check who wrote them. Reliability is not all-or-nothing, though: even a trusted newspaper can get one story wrong, so a careful evaluator still cross-checks an important fact rather than trusting any single source completely.

toolkit.title: Sentence starters for evaluating
toolkit.intro:
Use these to write clear evaluations of a source or argument:

And use these to write a balanced, justified judgement:
items: This source is reliable / unreliable because ...
The evidence is valid / invalid for this claim because ...
The author's purpose seems to be ..., which means ...
This source is biased because it ..., and the vested interest is ...
The argument is effective / weak because its reason ...
One point the other side gets right is ...
Having weighed both sides, I judge that ...
My strongest reason is ..., backed by ...
I accept that the other side is right that ...
However, on balance the stronger case is ..., because ...

checklists.title: Checklist: Is this fact real or fake?
checklists.intro: Use this whenever a source states a striking fact, especially one from an advert or a viral post. The more boxes you cannot tick, the more likely the fact is fake, so check it in a trusted source before you believe or share it.

challenge.intro:
Look back at the issues in the Lesson file, or think of your own. The best Evaluation Challenge is a question with real sources on both sides, such as 'Do energy drinks help students?' or 'Is this viral story true?' You want an argument to weigh, not a simple fact to look up.

A quick test for a good Evaluation Challenge: could two sensible people who both care about the truth still end up disagreeing? If yes, you have a question worth evaluating. If the answer can be settled in one search, it is a research question, not an evaluation one.
topics: Write your Challenge as a clear question: 'The question I am evaluating is ...'.
Write one sentence on why people disagree about it.
Name one source that says yes and one that says no, if you can.
checkpoints: I was surprised to discover that ...

activities.title: Analysis or evaluation?
activities.label: Activity 2: Analysis or evaluation?
activities.intro:
Evaluation builds on analysis but goes further, so first make sure you can tell them apart. For each sentence below, decide whether it is analysis (describing the parts) or evaluation (judging how good they are). Write A or E next to each.

Then write one sentence, in your own words, explaining the difference between analysis and evaluation.
steps: A. The article makes two claims and quotes one expert.
B. The article is weak because neither claim has any evidence.
C. The advert uses bright colours and a smiling face.
D. The advert is misleading because it hides the sugar content.
E. The report is reliable, since it comes from a health organisation with no product to sell.
F. The report is divided into three sections.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six answers to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it to explain any you got wrong, in a simple way.
Ask: What judging words are a clue that a sentence is evaluation, not analysis?

activities.title: Rate your sources for reliability and validity
activities.label: Activity 3: Rate your sources for reliability and validity
activities.intro:
Gather three or four sources on your Challenge, from different sides. For each one, judge two separate things: how reliable it is (can it be trusted?) and how valid its evidence is (does it really prove its claim?). Record your ratings in a table like the one below. Use high, medium or low, and add a short reason.

Filling this in makes your later judgement much easier, because your reasons are already written down. A source can score high on reliability but low on validity, so judge each column on its own. Do not give a source a high mark just because it is easy to read or agrees with you; mark it on who made it, what evidence it gives, and whether that evidence fits the claim.

boxes.title: A model: Maya rates one source
lines: Source: the shop poster, made by the drinks company, purpose to sell drinks.
Reliability: low, because it is unsigned, gives no real evidence, and no trusted source backs it.
Validity: low, because containing vitamins does not prove better exam results.
Maya writes both reasons in her journal, so her final judgement will be easy to defend.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your table to your AI tutor, source by source.
Ask it: Which of my sources is the strongest overall, and which is the weakest?
Ask the tutor whether any source I marked reliable is actually being used to prove something it does not prove.

activities.title: Real or fake? Check a fact
activities.label: Activity 4: Real or fake? Check a fact
activities.intro:
Find one striking 'fact' about your Challenge topic, the kind that appears in adverts or viral posts. Your job is to test whether it is real or fake by checking it against other sources, exactly as Maya did with the footballer claim.

For example, when Nadia saw a viral post claiming the sea had turned bright green along the Berbera coast, she did not share it in alarm. She first checked whether any trusted news source reported the same thing, and found none did. Checking before believing, and before sharing, is the whole skill.
steps: Write down the supposed fact and where you first saw it.
Search for the same fact in at least two trusted sources. List what you find.
Note who benefits if people believe the fact.
Give your judgement: real, fake, or not proven, with a reason.

boxes.title: Clues that a fact might be fake
lines: It appears on only one unknown website and nowhere trusted.
There is no named, real author, and the page is full of adverts.
It serves an obvious purpose, such as selling a product.
It sounds too dramatic, and no major news source mentions it.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Tell your AI tutor the supposed fact and what your checks turned up.
Ask it whether your evidence is enough to call the fact real, fake, or not proven.
Ask: What is one more check I could do before I rely on this fact?

activities.title: Sort fact from opinion
activities.label: Activity 5: Sort fact from opinion
activities.intro:
Strong evidence is built on facts, so practise telling facts from opinions. For each statement below, write F for a fact you could check or O for an opinion someone could dispute.

Then choose the two statements you think are the strongest evidence, and write one sentence explaining why facts usually beat unsupported opinions. Watch out for the trickiest kind: an opinion written in a confident voice so that it sounds like a fact. The word 'obviously' is often a warning sign that no evidence is coming.
steps: A. This drink contains 40 grams of sugar per can.
B. This is the best drink for students in the whole country.
C. Doctors at the health service recommend limiting sugary drinks.
D. Anyone who does not drink it will fall behind.
E. A study measured that the drink delays sleep by up to two hours.
F. Energy drinks are obviously perfectly safe.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your six labels to your AI tutor and ask it to check them.
Ask it why an expert opinion backed by facts can still be useful evidence.
Ask: In my own Challenge sources, which sentences are opinions pretending to be facts?

activities.title: Expose the bias and vested interest
activities.label: Activity 6: Expose the bias and vested interest
activities.intro:
Choose the most one-sided source you have found for your Challenge. Your task is to expose how it leans, and who gains.

Remember that having an interest does not make a source automatically wrong. It means you should balance it by finding a fair source from the other side. Write down where you could find that balancing source.

There is a difference between an honest purpose and hidden bias. A shop advert is allowed to want your custom; that is its honest purpose. It becomes biased only when it hides the drawbacks or is unfair to the other side. As you work, try to say clearly which of the two your source is doing, because that changes how much you can still trust it.
steps: Write down the source and its main message.
List the points it makes for its own side.
List any drawbacks or opposite points it leaves out.
Name who benefits if you believe it, and what their vested interest is.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Describe your one-sided source to your AI tutor and read out what it leaves out.
Ask it to help you name the vested interest behind the source.
Ask: Where could I find a trustworthy source from the opposite side to balance this one?

boxes.title: A human touch
lines: Show a family member an advert or post about your Challenge topic.
Ask them what they think it is trying to make people do, and what it leaves out.
Bring their answer to your next teacher session and compare it with your own.

activities.title: Find the claim, reason and evidence
activities.label: Activity 7: Find the claim, reason and evidence
activities.intro: Pick one argument about your Challenge, from either side. Break it into its three parts so you can judge each one.
steps: Write the claim: what is the argument trying to make you believe?
Write the reason: why does it say you should believe the claim?
Write the evidence: what facts, studies or examples back up the reason?
Judge each part: is the claim clear, does the reason fit, and is the evidence real and relevant?

boxes.title: A model, in case you get stuck
lines: Claim: Students should not drink energy drinks before exams.
Reason: because they disturb sleep, which harms memory.
Evidence: a health study measured worse sleep after drinking them.
Judgement: the reason fits the claim and the evidence is reliable, so this part of the argument is strong.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your claim, reason and evidence to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether the reason really justifies the claim.
Ask: Is the evidence strong enough, or is it just an opinion in disguise?

activities.title: Judge how effective an argument is
activities.label: Activity 8: Judge how effective an argument is
activities.intro:
Now judge a whole argument for effectiveness, and name its exact weakness. Below are four flawed arguments. For each, name the flaw (one-sided, unsupported, reason does not fit, or evidence does not prove it) and explain your choice.

Then rewrite one of them as a stronger, more honest argument, adding a real reason and better evidence, and admitting the other side where needed.
steps: Everyone in my class drinks it, so it must be good for studying.
This drink is amazing and will change your life. Just try it.
The drink contains vitamins, so it clearly boosts exam results.
This drink gives you energy, and it has no downsides at all.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your four flaw labels and your rewrite to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you named each flaw correctly.
Ask the tutor to argue back against your rewrite, then see if it still holds up.

activities.title: Weigh two competing arguments
activities.label: Activity 9: Weigh two competing arguments
activities.intro:
This is the heart of Stage 8 evaluation. Take the two strongest opposing arguments on your Challenge and weigh them side by side using the grid below. Fill in every box for both sides, then compare.

When both columns are full, write two sentences: which argument is stronger overall, and which point from the weaker side you still think is fair. Judging by the same tests on both sides is what makes your weighing honest.

rows: Main claim
Strongest reason
Quality of evidence
Reliability of source
Any bias or vested interest

boxes.title: A model: reading a finished grid
lines: Argument A, from the sellers: clear claim, reason keeps you awake, evidence only user reviews, source has a vested interest.
Argument B, from a health service: clear claim, reason harms sleep, evidence medical research, source has nothing to sell.
Judged by the same tests, Argument B is stronger overall.
The fair point kept from A: a very tired student may feel a short boost before the crash.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read both columns of your grid to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether you judged both sides by the same tests, or went easier on the side you prefer.
Ask: On this evidence, which argument is stronger, and by how much?

activities.title: Reach and justify your balanced judgement
activities.label: Activity 10: Reach and justify your balanced judgement
activities.intro:
Now bring everything together into one balanced, justified judgement on your Challenge. Use the four-part frame from the Lesson file, and lean on the evidence you have already gathered.

A balanced judgement is not a weak one. It is a decision that has looked the other side in the eye and still stands. Read yours aloud: could someone who disagrees with you at least see that you were fair?
steps: State your judgement: 'Having weighed both sides, I judge that ...'.
Give your strongest reason and the evidence behind it.
Admit the best point from the other side, fairly.
Explain why your side still wins overall.

boxes.title: What makes a judgement balanced
lines: It states a clear decision, not a vague 'both sides are fine'.
It rests on the strongest evidence, not on the side you liked first.
It names at least one fair point from the other side.
It explains why your side still wins overall.

boxes.title: Ask Your AI Tutor
lines: Read your full justified judgement to your AI tutor.
Ask it whether your reasons are backed by real evidence and whether you were fair to the other side.
Ask: Where is my judgement weakest, and how could I make it more convincing?

boxes.title: Bring it to your teacher
lines: Save your final judgement and the grid of evidence behind it.
Share them in your next teacher session and ask whether your judgement is balanced and well justified.

practice.intro: Answer these in your notebook or out loud with your AI tutor. There are 15 questions. Do not worry if some are tricky; that is how you find out what to practise next. Give your own words rather than copying from the other files.
practice.prompt: In your own words, what does 'evaluation' mean?
practice.answer: Evaluation means weighing the strengths and weaknesses of a source, argument or evidence to judge how far it can be trusted, then reaching a fair judgement. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

practice.prompt: What is the difference between analysis and evaluation?
practice.answer: Analysis breaks a thing into parts to understand it; evaluation judges how strong or trustworthy those parts are.

practice.prompt: A source that can be trusted to be true is called ______.
practice.answer: Reliable (reliability).

practice.prompt: Even if a fact is true, we must also ask whether it actually proves the claim. This is checking its ______.
practice.answer: Validity.

practice.prompt: In your own words, what is 'fake news'?
practice.answer: Fake news is false information deliberately created to trick people into believing it is true, often for political or business reasons.

practice.prompt: Name one good way to check whether a surprising fact is real or fake.
practice.answer: Any one of: check whether trusted sources report it; check for a real, named author; see who benefits; look for anything odd about the site or date.

practice.prompt: True or false: an opinion can never be used as evidence.
practice.answer: False. An opinion can be used as evidence, but it is weaker than a fact, especially if it has no facts behind it.

practice.prompt: When someone stands to gain money or power from you believing them, they have a ______ interest.
practice.answer: Vested.

practice.prompt: An argument has three parts: a claim, a reason, and ______.
practice.answer: Evidence.

practice.prompt: A reason answers 'Why do I think this?' What question does evidence answer?
practice.answer: It answers 'How do I know this?'

practice.prompt: An argument that gives only the advantages and hides the disadvantages is called ______.
practice.answer: One-sided.

practice.prompt: Name one thing an effective argument does that a weak one does not.
practice.answer: Any one of: gives reasons that truly justify the claim; backs them with reliable and relevant evidence; is honest about the other side.

practice.prompt: When you place two opposing arguments side by side and compare them, you are ______ them.
practice.answer: Weighing them.

practice.prompt: A balanced judgement should admit at least one good point from which side?
practice.answer: The other side (the weaker argument).

practice.prompt: Give one reason why being able to justify a judgement matters.
practice.answer: Any one of: it turns an opinion into a defendable conclusion; it lets others check your reasoning; it makes your judgement more convincing.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.intro: Match each evaluation word (1 to 6) to the correct meaning (A to F). Write the pairs, such as 1-C.
practice.prompt: Reliability
options: A. Whether a piece of evidence actually proves the particular claim it is used for.
B. A statement that something is true, which an argument then tries to support.
C. Whether a source can be trusted to be true and accurate.
D. Facts, studies or examples that back up a reason.
E. When a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
F. When a person or group stands to gain from you believing a claim.
practice.answer: C — Whether a source can be trusted to be true and accurate.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Validity
practice.answer: A — Whether a piece of evidence actually proves the particular claim it is used for.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Bias
practice.answer: E — When a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Vested interest
practice.answer: F — When a person or group stands to gain from you believing a claim.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Claim
practice.answer: B — A statement that something is true, which an argument then tries to support.

practice.partTitle: Match the word to its meaning
practice.prompt: Evidence
practice.answer: D — Facts, studies or examples that back up a reason.

practice.intro: These short scenarios ask you to use what you have learned. Write a sentence or two for each.
practice.prompt: Maya finds a claim on an unknown website that no news agency reports, on a page full of adverts. What should she suspect, and what should she do?
practice.answer: She should suspect it may be fake news, because it is unreported and the site profits from it. She should check trusted sources before believing or sharing it.

practice.prompt: An advert says a drink contains vitamins, so it must improve exam results. Is this a problem of reliability or of validity? Explain.
practice.answer: Validity. The fact about vitamins may be reliable, but it does not prove better exam results, so the evidence is invalid for that claim.

practice.prompt: Idris reads a leaflet from a company that praises its own product and mentions no drawbacks. What two things should he notice before trusting it?
practice.answer: He should notice the source has a vested interest in its own product, and that it is one-sided because it hides drawbacks. He should balance it with a fair source.

practice.prompt: Leila must weigh two arguments, one from a seller and one from a doctor, both with clear claims. What extra test helps her decide which to trust more?
practice.answer: She should check each argument's reliability and vested interest. The doctor has no product to sell, which makes that source more trustworthy than the seller.

practice.prompt: Omar writes: 'The drink is bad because I do not like it.' Why is this not a justified judgement, and how could he fix it?
practice.answer: It judges by personal taste, not evidence, so it is not justified. He could fix it by giving evidence, such as the drink's effect on sleep, and weighing both sides.

vocabulary.meaning: Weighing the strengths and weaknesses of a source or argument to judge how far it can be trusted.
Breaking a topic or source into parts to understand it, before you judge it.
Anywhere information comes from: a person, book, website, advert or video.
The person or organisation that made a source.
The reason a text was made, such as to inform, persuade, sell or entertain.
The group of people a text is aimed at.
Whether a source can be trusted to be true and accurate.
Whether a piece of evidence actually proves the particular claim it is used for.
A source that can be trusted to be true, often one you have heard of.
A source that cannot be trusted to be true.
False information deliberately created to trick people, often for political or business reasons.
Something that can be checked and proven to be true.
What someone thinks or believes, which others could reasonably dispute.
When a source leans unfairly to one side instead of being balanced.
When a person or group stands to gain from you believing a claim.
Giving only the advantages of something, and hiding the disadvantages.
A reason or set of reasons put forward to justify a claim, usually with evidence.
A statement that something is true, which an argument then tries to support.
Why a claim should be believed; it answers the question why do I think this?
Facts, studies, examples or quotations that back up a reason.
A certain view about or attitude towards a topic or issue.
An argument with a clear claim, fitting reasons, reliable evidence, and fairness to the other side.
To compare two arguments by the same tests to see which is stronger.
Your overall decision about how strong or trustworthy a source or argument is.
To give the reasons and evidence that support your judgement.
Fair to more than one side; a balanced judgement admits the other side's best point.
A notebook or file where you record your judgements and reasons as you go.

mistakes: Trusting a source just because you agree with it, or doubting one just because you do not.
Checking whether a fact is true but forgetting to ask whether it proves the claim.
Believing a striking 'fact' from one unknown site without checking trusted sources.
Mistaking a strongly stated opinion for a proven fact.
Ignoring who made a source and what they stand to gain.
Judging only one side instead of weighing both.
Reaching a judgement but giving no reasons to justify it.

questions.prompt: In your own words, what does 'evaluation' mean?
questions.modelAnswer: Evaluation means weighing the strengths and weaknesses of a source, argument or evidence to judge how far it can be trusted, then reaching a fair judgement. (Any answer with this idea is correct.)

questions.prompt: What is the difference between analysis and evaluation?
questions.modelAnswer: Analysis breaks a thing into parts to understand it; evaluation judges how strong or trustworthy those parts are.

questions.prompt: A source that can be trusted to be true is called ______.
Even if a fact is true, we must also ask whether it actually proves the claim. This is checking its ______.
In your own words, what is 'fake news'?
questions.modelAnswer: Fake news is false information deliberately created to trick people into believing it is true, often for political or business reasons.

questions.prompt: Name one good way to check whether a surprising fact is real or fake.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: check whether trusted sources report it; check for a real, named author; see who benefits; look for anything odd about the site or date.

questions.prompt: True or false: an opinion can never be used as evidence.
questions.modelAnswer: False. An opinion can be used as evidence, but it is weaker than a fact, especially if it has no facts behind it.

questions.prompt: When someone stands to gain money or power from you believing them, they have a ______ interest.
An argument has three parts: a claim, a reason, and ______.
A reason answers 'Why do I think this?' What question does evidence answer?
questions.modelAnswer: It answers 'How do I know this?'

questions.prompt: An argument that gives only the advantages and hides the disadvantages is called ______.
Name one thing an effective argument does that a weak one does not.
questions.modelAnswer: Any one of: gives reasons that truly justify the claim; backs them with reliable and relevant evidence; is honest about the other side.

selfAssessment.statement: I can explain what evaluation is and how it differs from analysis.
I can judge a source by its author and purpose.
I can tell reliability from validity and check both.
I can spot fake news and check whether a fact is real.
I can tell a fact from an opinion and judge their strength.
I can detect bias and vested interest in a source.
I can break an argument into claim, reason and evidence.
I can judge how effective an argument is and name its flaws.
I can weigh two competing arguments against each other.
I can reach a balanced judgement and justify it with reasons.
